No idea, but it's not too hard figuring this stuff out by yourself, that's what I did with this site at least..

Google the name of the publication, if it has a modicum of readers it'll have a Wikipedia entry which usually details owners, common criticisms etc..
That might get tricky with some papers, but googling the full "global research wikipedia" usually ends up in a result.

Rationalwiki and Conservapedia are also both to get a quick compass heading on shady sources.
Between these two, its simple: Google ranks Rationalwiki higher, and Google search ranking is pretty fucking robust at sorting information.

Anyway, the resulting wikipedia article is about the editor and not the paper or "institute" itself, which is a small warning sign. Jump down to criticism, and you instantly know the site's no good when this sentence appears:

Chussodovsky was said to hold that the U.S. had fore-knowledge of the September 11 attacks and the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami; that Washington had weapons that could influence climate change; and that the large banking institutions are the cause of the collapse of smaller economies, characterised by O'Neill as " more like wild-eyed conspiracy theories than serious political discourse".

Another and more common example or what to look for:
I had a discussion about what did and didn't happen at the fall of the Soviet Union and whether or not a certain promise was true or not, and I found this article which instantly debunked it citing Gorbachev himself: https://pressimus.com/Interpreter_Mag/stream/869

Again, googling the name "Interpreter_mag wikipedia" gets us this article about the magazines backer. The owners of the Institute have their own wiki articles, father is always more important and it doesn't take much skimming to see this guy has a rather strained relationship with Russia, the first sentence even mentioning he was formerly exiled.

Instant red flag, "Interpreter_mag" is not a trustworthy source.

If need be, parent companies, other names, board of directors etc all often tell small tales about possible biases, allegiances and hierarchies

An example of something positive:
https://consortiumnews.com/ is an independent site where the topic most often is contrary to the massmedia narratives. Not necessarily a bad thing that, but it should raise suspicion.

The articles here can often look like they're very pro-Moscow, and an obvious pro-anything usually isn't good.

Click About, and we see the editor is none other than Robert Parry. Keep reading and google him to verify: Seems this guy none other than one of those who exposed Iran-Contra, a long established truth. Perfect! Now we know it's very safe to assume you can trust what's being written on it. Keep investigating and you'll see the site is independent and funded by its readers.

All of this in combination is now something I can confidently use to take a massive shit on anyone trying to pull the shill-card on any of the articles or myself.
